title: The Continence of Scipio
text:
In 209 BC the young Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio captured New Carthage, the Carthaginian base in Spain. Among the prisoners, Livy says, his soldiers brought him a young woman of extraordinary beauty.

Scipio learned that she was engaged to a young Celtiberian chieftain named Allucius, who loved her deeply. He sent for her parents and her fiance. He told Allucius that she had been kept as carefully as if she were in her own parents' house, and that she was returned to him untouched. All he asked in return was that Allucius be a friend to the Roman people.

Her parents had brought a large sum of gold to ransom her. They begged Scipio to accept it as a gift. He had the gold laid at his feet, then gave it to Allucius as a wedding present.

Allucius went home and praised Scipio to his people as a godlike young man. A few days later, according to Livy, he returned to the Roman camp with fourteen hundred horsemen to serve under him. The historian Polybius tells a simpler version of the same story, without names. The scene was painted by many later artists as The Continence of Scipio.
lesson: Generosity toward the defeated can win loyalty that force never could. People remember how you treated them when you held all the power.
source: Livy, History of Rome 26.50; Polybius, Histories 10.19
caveat: The episode may have been polished by Roman writers to glorify Scipio.
